title: Where the Shuttle Crowding Actually Happens
text:
ARTICLE - Where the Shuttle Crowding Actually Happens

Harbor Tech operates a shuttle between its north parking lot and three office buildings. Employees have complained that the shuttle is “always overcrowded,” and an operations supervisor has proposed buying a second vehicle. Before approving the purchase, the facilities team reviewed four weeks of automatic passenger counts.

The counts show that crowding is concentrated in two short periods rather than spread across the day. The current shuttle has 24 seats. Facilities manager Mei Alvarez argues that the company should first add a second vehicle only during the morning arrival peak and the 5:00 p.m. departure peak, then measure whether riders are still left behind. She says an all-day second shuttle would cost substantially more while solving a problem the data show is mainly time-specific.

RIDERSHIP TABLE - Average passengers per trip

Time window | North lot to offices | Offices to north lot
7:30-8:30 a.m. | 29 | 6
8:30-10:00 a.m. | 18 | 5
10:00 a.m.-3:30 p.m. | 9 | 8
3:30-4:30 p.m. | 7 | 17
4:30-5:30 p.m. | 8 | 31
5:30-7:00 p.m. | 5 | 16

PASSENGER NOTE

“I usually take the 8:45 shuttle and can almost always sit down. Last Thursday I left early at 4:20 and there were several empty seats. My coworker takes the 5:05 shuttle and sometimes has to wait for the next trip.” - Employee comment submitted to facilities

Alvarez says the employee note is useful because it describes a pattern consistent with the counts, but she warns against treating one person’s experience as proof of system-wide conditions. The team also plans to count how often passengers are actually left behind, because a passenger total above 24 does not necessarily mean everyone was denied boarding; some riders may stand if vehicle rules permit it. The purchase decision will be reviewed after a six-week peak-hour trial.
